title: Microservices foundation (monolith vs microservices, service discovery, API gateway, saga, circuit breaker)
relevance: High — almost every HLD "design X" that grows past a single app box (e-commerce, ride-hailing, feeds); FAANG and Indian product cos probe when to split, how clients find instances, edge gateway vs LB, and how you keep consistency / survive dependency failure without claiming 2PC across services.
company_notes: Campus/intern/new-grad HLD: mention services, a gateway, and async boundaries in e-commerce, Uber/Ola, food delivery, Netflix — depth usually stops at tradeoffs plus one consistency/resilience pattern (saga or circuit breaker). Experienced/mid-level (1–4 YOE): discovery mode, BFF, saga choreography vs orchestration, breaker + timeout budgets, strangler migration, domain boundaries — common at Amazon, Uber, Meta, Flipkart, Atlassian. Frequency: near-universal as the shape of a scaled design; depth is tradeoffs and failure modes, not implementing Eureka or writing Hystrix.

phases.goal: Establish monolith vs microservices, when to split, and the microservice premium before any pattern talk.

must_hit.point: A monolith is one deployable unit with simpler transactions, debugging, and ops; microservices are independently deployable services around business capabilities, each often with its own datastore.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts single deployable unit vs independently deployable capability-aligned services with separate datastores.

must_hit.point: Microservices incur a microservice premium: ops, networking, observability, and distributed failure.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names ops/networking/observability/distributed-failure cost rather than only listing benefits.

must_hit.point: Default interview stance: start with a modular monolith; split when team/ownership/scale of change demands it — not when QPS alone spikes or as a fashion statement.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says start modular monolith and ties split to org/ownership/change cadence, not QPS fashion.

must_hit.point: Do not split when the team is small, domains are unclear, or there is no CI/CD or tracing — you get a distributed monolith.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate lists small team, unclear domains, missing CI/CD/tracing as reasons to stay monolith.

probes: For a startup checkout with 5 engineers versus Flipkart-scale catalog/orders/payments with separate teams, which architecture would you choose and what ops prerequisites would you demand before splitting?

hints.1: Think about team size and ownership first, not just traffic.
hints.2: Name the microservice premium and what CI/CD, monitoring, and provisioning you need before independent deploys.
hints.3: Start modular monolith for the small team; split only with clear bounded contexts, independent deploy cadence, and ops readiness — otherwise you ship a distributed monolith.

phases.goal: Explain how gateway, discovery, database-per-service, sagas, and circuit breakers actually work.

must_hit.point: API gateway is an L7 edge single entry for clients doing routing, authn/authz, rate limit, TLS, and sometimes aggregation/BFF — keep domain logic out of it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate places a thin L7 edge gateway with routing/auth/limits and refuses to put business workflows there.

must_hit.point: Service discovery: instances have dynamic IPs/ports; a registry holds healthy endpoints. Client-side: client queries registry and picks an instance. Server-side: client hits a stable router/LB/K8s Service that picks an instance; cloud default is server-side with health checks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate distinguishes client-side registry lookup vs server-side stable VIP/DNS (e.g. K8s Service) and mentions health checks.

must_hit.point: Database per service means private data behind APIs — no shared tables and no cross-service ACID; cross-service reads use API composition or CQRS views; cross-service writes use sagas.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate forbids shared DB/joins/2PC and routes cross-service writes to sagas (or boundary rethink).

must_hit.point: A saga is a sequence of local transactions; on failure run compensating transactions. Choreography uses events with no central boss; orchestration uses a central saga coordinator. Sagas are ACD with weak isolation — design for visible intermediate states and idempotent steps.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate walks local tx + compensations, names choreography vs orchestration, and notes weak isolation / intermediate states.

must_hit.point: Circuit breaker wraps remote calls: Closed (pass through, count failures) → Open (fail fast / fallback) → Half-Open (probe); stops cascading failure and thread/connection pile-up on timeouts.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate sketches Closed → Open → Half-Open and links it to fail-fast and preventing cascade/resource exhaustion.

probes: Walk place-order as reserve inventory → charge payment → create shipment: if payment succeeds and a later step fails, how do choreography vs orchestration run compensating actions, and why isn't this distributed 2PC?

hints.1: Each service only does a local transaction — what undoes a completed step?
hints.2: Contrast event-driven next steps versus a central coordinator commanding steps; name compensations like refund or release inventory.
hints.3: Say local txs + compensations (saga), not cross-service rollback; mention ACD/weak isolation and idempotent steps instead of 2PC ACID across services.

phases.goal: Force clear choices among gateway vs LB, discovery modes, sync vs async, and coordination styles.

must_hit.point: API gateway is not an L4 load balancer: the gateway understands HTTP semantics (path routing, auth, aggregation); an LB spreads identical backends — a plain LB is enough when you only need to spread identical instances.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate separates L7 gateway concerns from L4 LB fan-out and says when LB alone suffices.

must_hit.point: Sync RPC (HTTP/gRPC) fits request/response on the critical path; async messaging fits fan-out, decoupling, and long workflows — do not turn every call into Kafka.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate picks sync for critical-path request/response and async for fan-out/long workflows without making everything a queue.

must_hit.point: Saga choreography can get tangled without a central boss; orchestration is clearer for complex flows but the coordinator is a failure/ops concern.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate trades choreography tangle risk against orchestration clarity and coordinator as a single ops/failure point.

must_hit.point: Retries without a circuit breaker can amplify outages; pair breakers with timeouts, retries with jitter, and bulkheads.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate warns that bare retries amplify load and names timeouts, jittered retries, and bulkheads alongside the breaker.

probes: A mobile app needs auth, path routing (/orders vs /payments), and response aggregation — draw edge boxes and say what sits where; when is a plain LB enough?

hints.1: Separate the client-facing edge from spreading identical backends.
hints.2: Put auth, path routing, and aggregation on an L7 gateway; put instance fan-out on an LB or service layer.
hints.3: Gateway = L7 single entry (routing/auth/limits/aggregation/BFF); LB = spread identical backends — plain LB enough when you only need that fan-out.

phases.goal: Apply strangler migration, discovery under churn, and resilience patterns in concrete HLD scenarios.

must_hit.point: Migrate with Strangler Fig: put a facade/gateway in front of the monolith, peel routes to new services gradually, retire the old path when traffic is gone — prefer over big-bang rewrite.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes gateway-fronted incremental route extraction and rollback by sending traffic back to the old path.

must_hit.point: For many pods with changing IPs (e.g. 50 order-service pods), prefer cloud-default server-side discovery (K8s Service / cloud LB) plus health checks; on a bad deploy, unhealthy instances are removed from the pool.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate picks server-side discovery with health checks and explains bad instances dropping out of the healthy set.

must_hit.point: If a payment provider's p95 latency spikes to 30s, without a breaker threads/connections and upstream latency die first; with Closed → Open → Half-Open, fail fast and use a fallback such as queue for retry, pay later, or a cached quote.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names thread/connection pile-up, sketches breaker states, and gives a concrete payment fallback.

must_hit.point: Blast-radius lesson: one service down should degrade (cached/default response), not take the product down; at Uber scale, manage domains of related services with gateways — not thousands of orphan nanoservices.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate talks degrade-not-die and domain-oriented grouping rather than infinite nanoservices.

probes: Extract notifications from a monolith with Strangler Fig: where does the gateway route before, during, and after cutover, and how do you roll back?

hints.1: Something sits in front of the monolith before any code moves.
hints.2: Route only the notifications path to the new service while other paths still hit the monolith.
hints.3: Before: all via facade to monolith; during: notifications route to new service, rest to monolith; after: old notifications path retired; rollback = point that route back to the monolith.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Monolith: one deployable unit, simpler tx/debugging/ops. Microservices: independent deploy around business capabilities and often private datastores, but pay the microservice premium (ops, networking, observability, distributed failure). Start modular monolith; split for independent deploy cadence, different scaling profiles, clear bounded contexts, and blast-radius isolation — not for small teams, unclear domains, or missing CI/CD/tracing.

tradeoffs.topic: API gateway vs L4 load balancer
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Gateway is L7 single entry: routing, authn/authz, rate limit, TLS, sometimes aggregation/BFF; keep domain logic out. LB spreads identical backends. Use gateway when clients need HTTP-aware edge behavior; plain LB when you only need to fan out to identical instances.

Client-side: client queries the registry and picks a healthy instance (Ribbon/Eureka-style). Server-side: client calls a stable router/LB/K8s Service that chooses an instance. Cloud interview default is server-side discovery with health checks.

Both: local transactions plus compensating transactions on failure (not cross-service DB rollback). Choreography: events trigger next steps, no central boss, can get tangled. Orchestration: central coordinator commands steps — clearer for complex flows, but the coordinator is a failure/ops concern. Expect ACD with weak isolation and visible intermediate states.
Sync HTTP/gRPC for request/response on the critical path; async messaging for fan-out, decoupling, and long workflows. Do not turn every inter-service call into a queue.

gotchas.trap: Drawing many microservices (e.g. 12) for a campus URL shortener / over-engineering a Netflix clone.
gotchas.correction: Interviewers want judgment: start modular monolith; split only when ownership and change demand it.

gotchas.trap: Shared database "for convenience" while calling the design microservices.
gotchas.correction: That is a distributed monolith — you paid the network cost without deploy/data independence; use database per service.

gotchas.trap: Claiming exactly-once delivery or full ACID across Order + Payment + Inventory via 2PC.
gotchas.correction: Prefer saga + idempotency + eventual consistency; 2PC across services is painful.

gotchas.trap: API gateway that embeds business workflows.
gotchas.correction: It becomes a new monolith and deploy bottleneck; keep the gateway thin (routing, auth, limits).

gotchas.trap: Retries without idempotency keys and without a circuit breaker.
gotchas.correction: Risk of double charges and thundering herds; pair idempotency with breaker, timeouts, and jittered retries.

gotchas.trap: Forgetting observability (correlation IDs, tracing, metrics) across N services.
gotchas.correction: Debugging is otherwise hopeless — treat observability as part of the microservice premium.
K8s runs whatever you package; choosing monolith vs microservices is a separate architecture decision.
